Durable conventions and project facts, for any engineer or agent working in this repo.

## Core principles (P1–P8, cited by number)

- **P1 — Attention-first.** Human attention is the scarcest resource; a gate, pause or escalation that does not change an outcome is ceremony and must be removed.
- **P2 — The knowledge base is the product.** Every unit of work consumes accumulated knowledge and produces it. The test for a feature: does it improve what we capture, or how well we retrieve it?
- **P3 — Scripts over agents.** Deterministic code unless the work provably needs judgment; code cannot drift or forget.
- **P4 — Lifecycle-bound state.** Transient state is removed by the event that ends its life; durable value is promoted before disposal, never by a remembered step.
- **P5 — Fail loud, never silent.** Unknown signals halt. Missing inputs block. A degraded path announces that it is degraded.
- **P6 — Maximal *relevant* context.** Every agent operates with all knowledge bearing on its task, retrieved filter-first and capped; starving and flooding are both failures.
- **P7 — Prevention over recovery.** Over-scoping is a decomposition failure: re-scope and redo rather than build resume machinery.
- **P8 — Match mechanism to work.** Judgment gets strong models; mechanical work gets cheap models or scripts.

## Knowledge (generated projections)

- **The knowledge base is projected into the repo.** `architecture.md` says what each area does and which files it owns; `rulings.md` lists every decision and anti-pattern that governs the code. Read the entries for an area before touching it. Both are generated by the Sterling operator and never hand-edited; if you find them wrong, say so in your commit message rather than editing them.

## Conduct rules

- **Anti-speculation:** never invent an API, field, flag, or behavior; cite tool-call evidence from this turn, or say "I don't know, checking" and check.
- **No false action claims:** never imply something was saved, run, recorded, or changed unless it was actually performed this turn with evidence.
- **Lint and tests before done.** Before reporting a code change done, run this project's lint/format command (under Project facts) and the tests for what changed. Red lint is a blocker, not a note. If no lint/format command is recorded, say so in the report, and once you know the command add a `Lint/format command:` line under Project facts.
- **Write plainly; no AI tells.** Prose for people (docs, READMEs, store records, commit and PR text, UI copy, reports) says specific things in ordinary words: is/has rather than serves as/boasts, no em-dash chains, no "not just X, it's Y", no puffed-up significance, no stock AI vocabulary (delve, pivotal, robust, tapestry), no "it's important to note" or "In conclusion". Keep every fact; never invent detail to replace filler. Perfect grammar and a formal tone are not tells, so leave clean sentences alone. The full catalogue is Wikipedia's *Signs of AI writing*.
- **Text meant to be copied goes between two horizontal rules.** When you hand the user something to paste elsewhere (a prompt for another session, a message, an issue body), introduce it with one line saying where it goes ("Paste this as the first message in …"), then put the text alone between a `---` line before and after it. The text is self-contained: it assumes the reader has none of this conversation, quotes the user's words where they matter, and names files, ids and rules explicitly. Use plain markdown inside, not a code fence, unless the text is code or a command. Notes about the text go after the closing rule, never inside it. (User-ruled 2026-10-24 after a kick-start prompt for the Overpass project: "make it the standard way of doing copy friendly text"; decision `copy-friendly-text-a-prompt-or-message-for-the-user-to-paste`.)
- **Start every subagent and every long shell command in the background.** Keep reporting and do work that does not depend on the lanes while they run, and act on each lane when its completion notification arrives. On OpenCode, pass `background: true` on every `subagent` call, so the user never has to press ctrl+B; OpenCode V2 has no setting that makes background the default (its agent docs list none), so the flag goes on each call. A shell command that may take more than about 20 seconds (a test suite such as `npm test` or `dotnet test`, a build, a deploy, `pr-review-wait`, `gh run watch`, a setup chain in a worktree) starts the same way, because the host notifies the session when it ends: OpenCode takes `background: true` on its shell tool, Claude Code `run_in_background`. Never wait with a foreground `sleep`, `sleep N; tail …` or a polling loop: start the work in the background, do other work, and let the completion notice resume you. This is the rule for the main session; a lane waiting on its own targeted test result runs it in the foreground (decision `lanes-run-targeted-tests-in-foreground-conductor-quiet-on-empty-notifications`). Short reads stay in the foreground. A conductor parked on a foreground shell or sleep does nothing while it runs: in five days Customer Hub conductors ran 29 foreground shells over 60 s and 110 foreground `sleep`/`tail` polls (finding `why-do-customer-hub-ch-conductors-sit-waiting-while-shells-r`). User-stated 2026-10-25, verbatim: "Update instructions about having tasks and stuff running in the background to also include shells. Currently customer hub projects are just waiting while shells are running". User-stated 2026-10-15 (GitHub issue #95): "always start everything in the background if possible". User-ruled 2026-10-09 through the question form, "Add it to CLAUDE.md (Recommended)", after the user asked (verbatim): "Can I choose a setting to always spawn the subagents in the background and not have to press to ctrl+B?"; restated 2026-10-10 (verbatim): "Also make sure that it is stated in the agents.md that all subagents are run in the background."
- **Finish what you start.** Carry each started task to its end state (committed, pushed or merged as the project's flow says, review comments answered and resolved, records updated) before ending a turn. When only an outside wait is left (a review bot, a build), run it in the background as above, so it notifies you when it ends; only where the host cannot notify, check it in short foreground rounds. Never use a detached process (`nohup … &`) that cannot report back; if the turn must end, say plainly what is awaited (GitHub issue #79, 2026-10-12: turns ended with fixes uncommitted, and a Copilot review sat unanswered for about 45 minutes after a detached wait died silently).
- **Resolve a review thread once its finding is handled.** When a review finding is fixed (fix pushed, reply posted) or disagreed with (reason posted), resolve its thread: a reply does not resolve it, and branch protection that requires resolved conversations keeps the PR blocked while any thread is open. Leave a thread open while its finding waits on a user ruling (GitHub issues #42 and #78).
- **An index or summary is a lookup, never a source.** A digest line, a quotation inside another record — these LOCATE the source; they never replace it. A cited line number is an instruction to OPEN THE FILE: the binding constraint often lives in the prose around the quoted line, which is exactly what the summary dropped.
- **Read before edit; grep callers before changing a signature.**
- **Minimal change:** smallest safe implementation; no speculative abstractions; no unrelated cleanup; prefer existing patterns. No drive-by refactors, no "while I'm here" improvements. One concern per change. **Does not override** consolidating a mechanism you are ALREADY modifying — on a third-or-later change to it, consolidating is the smallest total change, and boarding it is the drive-by.
- **Rebuild over patch.** A fix growing out of proportion to its defect stops and rebuilds from blank: *is the fix removing the cause, or adding handlers for its effects?* Freeze the pins (existing plus the new findings), state the invariant in one paragraph including what it does NOT guarantee, rebuild against those pins, read the old file only afterwards to check nothing was dropped. **Does not override** minimal-change for a first defect.
- **Surface smells, don't fix them.** When you hit bad code or a design smell outside the current task, surface it as a separate issue — never fix it inline (minimal-change holds), never stay silent. Whether to track it is the user's call, not a drive-by.
- **Ask, don't guess. One question at a time** — the single most important question, with options and a recommendation; never batch questions. Where a prompt may time out unanswered, prefer the safe default and proceed, disclosing the assumption — but ONLY for a reversible choice needing no authorization, and NEVER for a gate/grill decision, which is re-asked or waited out instead.
- **A rule stated at full force carries its own fence.** Any rule strong enough to be cited AGAINST another rule states, immediately beneath it, what it does NOT override — plus the test for when the two genuinely pull against each other: does the cautious step protect against something EXPENSIVE OR IRREVERSIBLE? Then take it. Does it merely make you MORE CONFIDENT about something the suite is about to tell you anyway? Then skip it and build.
- **Never self-verify.** A code-touching diff gets an independent reviewer — the author of a change is never its checker. Review happens **sparsely, once a task is done**: one reviewer (3 to 5 parallel reviewers in a work-mode project, before the PR) over the riskiest part of the whole branch's diff plus every changed test in full, never per edit and never per commit. This is a practice, not a hook — nothing mechanically catches a skipped review, which is exactly why you do not skip it.
- **Propose a better way.** You are a reasoning partner, not a note-taker. When you see an approach that materially beats the one asked for, say so before implementing — but only when it changes an outcome (avoids irreversible work, data loss, a security hole, broad rework), never for a prettier abstraction. Give the better path, the risk it protects, the tradeoff, and how to verify; then proceed with the asked path unless told otherwise.
- **Disclose limitations, don't bury them.** A known limitation that weakens or defeats what the work is *for* is raised as an explicit keep-or-solve decision **before** you build. "It opens but can't do X" is unfit-for-purpose, not done-with-a-note.
- **Verbatim intent capture.** Intent-capture surfaces receive the user's words VERBATIM — no paraphrase, no pre-stuffing, no helpful tidying. A paraphrase silently substitutes your model of the intent for theirs.
- **Never ship:** hardcoded secrets or credentials; swallowed errors, bare catch-alls or silent fallbacks that mask a real failure; weakened, skipped or deleted tests to make a suite green; leftover debug output or commented-out code unless a stub was asked for.

## Domains

- **A domain is a shared knowledge store for one subject.** It is kept per user, outside any repo, and every project on the machine that mounts it reads and writes the same store. A project mounts the domains named in its stack tags.
- **Mount every subject the project works with, its own subject included.** Two projects share knowledge only through a domain both mount.
- **What not to do:** a Salesforce project that mounts only `genesys` and a Genesys project that mounts only `salesforce` share nothing, because no domain is mounted by both. Both should mount `salesforce` and `genesys`.
- **A domain needs a description** that says which knowledge belongs in it. The description decides where a new record is written and what gets promoted into the domain.
- **Run `/sterling:domains` to see and change mounts.** It lists every domain on this machine with the projects that mount it, shows what this project shares with each other project, and adds a missing domain after you agree. It never removes one.

## Conventions (lean — grows only via architecture-altering decision records)

- **No hand-maintained architecture or design documents.** Generated projections only, clearly marked. Knowledge lives in the store; a document that duplicates it will drift from it, and the copy is always the one that lies.

## Godot and Blender conventions (ported from Dome Farmer)

These rules were learned on Dome Farmer, a Godot and Blender project on the same machine. They are adapted to this game: a Godot 4.7.2 project in `game/`, with assets from the Toon Series packs. The graphics and physics agent is `.claude/agents/implementor-graphic.md`; the asset method is `.claude/skills/blender-asset/SKILL.md`; the test method is `.claude/skills/test-writing/SKILL.md`.

### Visual inspection and plates

- **Open every image a subagent produces before repeating a claim about it.** For motion, open rendered frame strips. An agent's numbers are structure evidence only. The sentence "it looks correct" is the one claim an agent could not have verified.
- **Read the whole plate, not only the fix.** Check that each effect starts at its true source, every part is attached, nothing floats, doubles, clips, is oversized or is missing, and the subject is big enough to judge. A subject a few pixels tall is not inspected; re-frame it. Write one line per plate naming what was checked.
- **Structure and appearance are different questions.** Vertex counts, bounding boxes and UV asserts say nothing about how an asset looks. A mean-colour figure is not evidence either.
- **Require six-axis orthographic views at true scale with a 1 m reference cube, plus a distance shot.** Legibility at range is usually the real requirement.
- **A new on-screen element uses its ruled form.** Before a brief names a marker, ghost, highlight, colour or caption, find the rulings for that element and quote them in the brief.
- **Every generated plate goes under `tools/blender/out/<purpose>/`, which is gitignored.** Never put a plate in a tracked directory.
- **The Blender view is never the authority on in-engine appearance.** Assets can pass every Blender check and still render wrong in the game. Only a windowed Godot render answers whether it looks right, and the Unity toon shaders are rebuilt in Godot, so check the ramp and outline there.

### Probes

- A probe is a script that `extends SceneTree`: `_initialize()` sets up, `_process(delta) -> bool` is a frame-driven state machine that returns `true` to quit. To drive the real game, `load("res://main.tscn").instantiate()`, set any `@export` BEFORE `add_child` (instantiating does not run `_ready()`; entering the tree does), then step frames and give each stage a settle window.
- **Write probes that cannot pass by accident.** Every pass value is a positive (a count that grew, a position that moved), and each prints the values it compared, not a verdict. If the pass value is a zero, add a control proving the subject was engaged.
- **Every plate proves its subject is in frame before it is saved.** Project the subject with `camera.unproject_position(subject.global_position)`, assert the point falls inside the viewport with a margin, and print the coordinates. Then check occlusion with a raycast, because in-frame is not visible. On failure print `PROBE_INVALID` and exit 1. A colour statistic cannot do this job.
- A probe boots the real game with a new random world seed and prints it, so a failure can be replayed.

### Godot run modes

- **Godot has four run modes and they are not interchangeable.** `--check-only` is the parse gate. The gdUnit4 suite is for logic. `--headless -s <script>` is for a spike. `--path game ... -s <script>` windowed is for anything the GPU owns. A test that does not build the real scene cannot find a composition bug, so a probe is the floor for `main.tscn`.
- **gdUnit4:** `--ignoreHeadlessMode` is mandatory (without it gdUnit4 refuses to run and exits 103, which reads like a crash). Exit 0 is a pass, 100 is failures, 105 means a test suite failed to parse (for example a class it uses does not exist yet). Pass `-c` so a fail-fast does not hide most of the failures. Put `--ignoreHeadlessMode` after `-s res://addons/gdUnit4/bin/GdUnitCmdTool.gd` and the `-a` arguments; placed before the script it exits 103. A suite that fails to parse can also hang with no exit code instead of exiting 105, so run test commands under `timeout`.
- **Every Godot run the user does not play passes `--audio-driver Dummy`**, so test sound does not play on the user's speakers.
- **Windowed runs need `--display-driver windows --rendering-driver vulkan`.** Headless loads the dummy rendering server, so a GPU-backed render or timing taken there is a broken instrument.
- **Exactly one windowed Godot run at a time, project-wide.** Two at once corrupt the import cache and lose every render in flight. Batch subjects into one run and hold the slot yourself. A game launched through the Godot MCP holds the slot too.
- **Import is mandatory after adding or moving any `.gd`**, and after re-exporting an asset into `game/`, before any test or render.
- Run the full suite once on the final tree before a merge, not on every commit. A commit needs the fast gates on the touched files (`--check-only`, `gdlint`, `gdformat --check`) and the targeted tests with their case counts.

### Blender work

- **Build work is always `--background --python`.** Headless is reproducible (the command line goes into the report), runs in parallel across processes and leaves no residual state. The Blender MCP is for inspection only and is never the authority on appearance.
- **Rebind the Toon palette atlas on import.** A skipped rebind fails silently and exports an untextured mesh. Check the image and material counts in the export's own output.
- **Verify an export by re-reading the written file, not the scene.** A glTF that flattened its node hierarchy looks identical in a still. Put each origin on its own rotation axis.
- **The render is the only test that counts for appearance.**

### MCP mechanics

- The Godot server is `godot-mcp-runtime`, launched by `tools/godot-mcp-wsl.sh` on Windows node. Tool calls pass the Windows project path `C:/Users/chulf/Gotta-make-my-flight/game`. The server writes `game/.mcp/` and does not remove it on stop. The Blender server is launched by `tools/blender-mcp-wsl.sh`. Both are declared in `.mcp.json`.
- **Where the Godot MCP has no tool for a job, say so in the report, name the tool you looked for, and use the direct command.** Check the tool list at the start of the task. It cannot run an `-s` SceneTree probe.
- **Godot:** scene-editing tools refuse while a game runs, so call `stop_project` first. `get_debug_output` works only for a game started by `run_project`. Take screenshots with `responseMode: 'path_only'` unless you need pixel-exact output. One broken autoload fails every headless tool; check `list_autoloads` first. A key or action input without `pressed` taps it; set `pressed` to hold. Never set `GODOT_MCP_DISABLE_SECURITY`.
- **Blender:** `execute_blender_code` returns only what the code assigns to `result` (a JSON-serialisable dict); printed output is lost. Set mode, active object and selection before each operator. Call `view_layer.update()` before reading world matrices or modifier results, and flush bmesh edits. Keep the object reference at creation, because names gain `.001` on collision. `render_viewport_to_path` ignores the directory and writes to Blender's temp folder, so copy the plate under `tools/blender/out/`. The server adds no undo step, so save the `.blend` before a change you may need to reverse.

### Machine facts

- **Godot** is at `/mnt/c/Users/chulf/AppData/Local/Programs/Godot/`. From WSL bash use `Godot_v4.7.2-stable_win64_console.exe`; a `C:/...` path as the executable exits 127.
- **Blender** is at `/mnt/c/Program Files/Blender Foundation/Blender 5.2/`. The path contains spaces, so quote it.
- **There is no `python` in WSL.** A bare `python` hits the Windows Store alias and exits 49. Blender work uses Blender's own bundled interpreter. For a one-off JSON read, use `node -e`, `grep` or `sed`.
- **gdtoolkit** (`gdlint.exe`, `gdformat.exe`) is at `/mnt/c/Users/chulf/.local/bin/`, not in the WSL `~/.local/bin`. `gdformat.exe` writes CRLF line endings when it rewrites a file; convert back to the file's own endings.
- **Subagent shells** may be unable to run `unzip`, `mkdir`, `cp` or `find`. Extracting a vendor archive is then a conductor step; hand agents the extracted path.

### The gdlint line cap

- `gdlintrc` sets `max-file-lines: 1600` and the check counts comments as well as code. `max-public-methods` is 20 and `max-returns` is 6.
- An exemption is per file, never a bigger number in `gdlintrc`: put `# gdlint:disable = max-file-lines` in the file. The spelling matters, because `max-file-lines` responds only to `disable`, not `ignore`.
- Never trust a written list of exempt files. `grep -rlnE "gdlint:disable *=.*max-file-lines" game --include=*.gd` is the only authority.
- New behaviour goes in a new file, not in headroom under the cap.

### Parallelism by territory

- Two agents must never write the same file; disjoint files parallelise freely. A lane is one territory (for example `game/` code, `game/tests/`, `tools/blender/`), not one agent. Refill a territory the moment its lane reports.
- **File-disjoint is not scene-disjoint.** An agent editing a script that `main.tscn` reaches blocks every lane's probe on `main.tscn`. Ask which scenes a writer's file is reachable from.
- Serialise windowed Godot runs. Blender headless renders parallelise and write `tools/blender/`, never `game/`. Git stays conductor-only.
